claim: Cell competition is a fitness control mechanism in which less fit cells (the losers) are eliminated from a tissue for optimal survival of the host.
source: Cell competition is a fitness control mechanism in which less fit cells (the losers) are eliminated from a tissue for optimal survival of the host (Vincent et al., 2013; Levayer and Moreno, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vincent et al., 2013 and Levayer and Moreno, 2013.

claim: Cell competition was first discovered in the Drosophila wing disc.
source: First discovered in the Drosophila wing disc (Morata and Ripoll, 1975), cell competition has since been observed in many other physiological and pathophysiological contexts, especially in embryogenesis (Amoyel and Bach, 2014) and the development of tumours (Chen et al., 2012; Madan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morata and Ripoll, 1975.

claim: Cell competition has been observed in embryogenesis and the development of tumours.
source: First discovered in the Drosophila wing disc (Morata and Ripoll, 1975), cell competition has since been observed in many other physiological and pathophysiological contexts, especially in embryogenesis (Amoyel and Bach, 2014) and the development of tumours (Chen et al., 2012; Madan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amoyel and Bach, 2014; Chen et al., 2012; and Madan et al., 2019.

claim: Mechanical competition arises because loser cells are more sensitive to crowding than winners.
source: Mechanical competition arises because loser cells are more sensitive to crowding than winners (Shraiman, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shraiman, 2005.

claim: During mechanical competition, loser cells die cell-autonomously because the overall cell density is increased by the growth of winners.
source: Losers are thought to die cell-autonomously because the overall cell density is increased by the growth of winners and, as a result, loser cells far from the interface with winners may die (Wagstaff et al., 2016; Levayer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wagstaff et al., 2016 and Levayer et al., 2016.

claim: During biochemical competition, signalling occurs at the interface between cell types leading to apoptosis of loser cells only when in direct contact with winners.
source: By contrast, during biochemical competition, signalling occurs at the interface between cell types leading to apoptosis of loser cells only when in direct contact with winners (Moreno et al., 2002; Yamamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moreno et al., 2002 and Yamamoto et al., 2017.

claim: In biochemical competition, the probability of elimination depends on the extent of contact a loser cell has with the winners.
source: Here, the probability of elimination depends on the extent of contact a loser cell has with the winners (Levayer et al., 2015; Díaz-Díaz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Levayer et al., 2015 and Díaz-Díaz et al., 2017.

claim: Perturbations affecting the strength of intercellular adhesions strongly affect the outcome of biochemical competition.
source: As a result, perturbations affecting the strength of intercellular adhesions strongly affect the outcome of competition, suggesting that cell mixing is an important factor in biochemical competition (Levayer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levayer et al., 2015.

claim: Loser cell death in mechanical competition is strongly influenced by local cell density.
source: For example, recent work has shown that loser cell death in an experimental model system for mechanical competition is strongly influenced by local cell density as expected, but that, in addition, division of winner cells appears favoured in neighbourhoods with many loser cells, something reminiscent of biochemical competition (Bove et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bove et al., 2017.

claim: Division of winner cells appears favoured in neighbourhoods with many loser cells.
source: For example, recent work has shown that loser cell death in an experimental model system for mechanical competition is strongly influenced by local cell density as expected, but that, in addition, division of winner cells appears favoured in neighbourhoods with many loser cells, something reminiscent of biochemical competition (Bove et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bove et al., 2017.

claim: The multi-scale agent-based model can replicate competition when two distinct cell types are mixed.
source: After calibrating the behaviour of winner and loser cells based on movies of pure cell populations, we show that we can replicate competition when the two distinct cell types are mixed and investigate the impact of each interaction and kinetic parameters on the outcome of mechanical cell competition.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the model's capabilities in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanical competition is controlled by the difference in homeostatic density between cell types.
source: We find that mechanical competition appears to be controlled by the difference in homeostatic density between cell types, whereas biochemical competition is governed by tissue organisation.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Biochemical competition is governed by tissue organisation.
source: We find that mechanical competition appears to be controlled by the difference in homeostatic density between cell types, whereas biochemical competition is governed by tissue organisation.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: A key determinant of mechanical competition is the difference in homeostatic density between winners and losers.
source: We find that a key determinant of mechanical competition is the difference in homeostatic density between winners and losers, while differences in growth rates and tissue organisation do not affect competition end result.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differences in growth rates and tissue organisation do not affect mechanical competition end result.
source: We find that a key determinant of mechanical competition is the difference in homeostatic density between winners and losers, while differences in growth rates and tissue organisation do not affect competition end result.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: When loser cells are homogenously mixed with winners at the onset of competition, they are eradicated in biochemical competition.
source: Indeed, when loser cells are homogenously mixed with winners at the onset of competition, they are eradicated; however, when they are spatially separated, winner and loser cells coexist for long times.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: When loser cells are spatially separated from winners at the onset of competition, winner and loser cells coexist for long times in biochemical competition.
source: Indeed, when loser cells are homogenously mixed with winners at the onset of competition, they are eradicated; however, when they are spatially separated, winner and loser cells coexist for long times.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanical and biochemical modes of cell competition have distinct biophysical origins.
source: These findings suggest distinct biophysical origins for mechanical and biochemical modes of cell competition.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the results of the computational model.

claim: MDCK cells maintain cell size homeostasis by following an 'adder' mechanism.
source: Experimental work has shown that MDCK cells maintain cell size homeostasis by following an 'adder' mechanism, in which each cell cycle adds a set volume to the cell (Cadart et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cadart et al., 2018.

claim: In the adder mechanism, each cell cycle adds a set volume to the cell.
source: Experimental work has shown that MDCK cells maintain cell size homeostasis by following an 'adder' mechanism, in which each cell cycle adds a set volume to the cell (Cadart et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cadart et al., 2018.

claim: Contact inhibition of proliferation is a phenomenon where proliferation ceases above a certain cell density.
source: Above a certain cell density, proliferation ceases – a phenomenon known as contact inhibition of proliferation (Abercrombie, 1979; Lieberman and Glaser, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abercrombie, 1979 and Lieberman and Glaser, 1981.

claim: Arrest in proliferation due to contact inhibition is accompanied by a decrease in protein synthesis due to a drop in ribosome assembly and downregulation of the synthesis of cyclins.
source: Arrest in proliferation is accompanied by a decrease in protein synthesis due to a drop in ribosome assembly and downregulation of the synthesis of cyclins (Azar et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Azar et al., 2010.

claim: Cell elimination can occur through live cell extrusions when the cell apical area decreases substantially compared to the population average.
source: In experiments, cell elimination can also occur through live cell extrusions when the cell apical area decreases substantially compared to the population average (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Kocgozlu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eisenhoffer et al., 2012 and Kocgozlu et al., 2016.

claim: Epithelia possess a preferred density to which they return following perturbation, signifying that they seek to maintain a homeostatic density.
source: Previous work has revealed that epithelia possess a preferred density to which they return following perturbation, signifying that they seek to maintain a homeostatic density (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012; Gudipaty et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012; and Gudipaty et al., 2017.

claim: When deformation increased cellular apical area, the frequency of cell division increased.
source: When deformation increased cellular apical area, the frequency of cell division increased (Gudipaty et al., 2017), while a decrease in apical area resulted in increased live cell extrusion and apoptosis (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gudipaty et al., 2017.

claim: A decrease in apical area resulted in increased live cell extrusion and apoptosis.
source: When deformation increased cellular apical area, the frequency of cell division increased (Gudipaty et al., 2017), while a decrease in apical area resulted in increased live cell extrusion and apoptosis (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eisenhoffer et al., 2012.

claim: In experiments on confluent MDCKWT epithelia, a sudden increase in crowding was followed by a gradual decrease in cell density resulting from a combination of apoptoses and live cell extrusion, before returning to the initial homeostatic density after ∼6 hr.
source: In experiments on confluent MDCKWT epithelia (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012), a sudden increase in crowding was followed by a gradual decrease in cell density resulting from a combination of apoptoses and live cell extrusion, before returning to the initial homeostatic density after ∼6 hr (green data points, Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eisenhoffer et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The model implementation and parametrisation replicate the return to homeostasis of pure populations of MDCKWT cells.
source: Thus, our model implementation and parametrisation replicate the return to homeostasis of pure populations of MDCKWT cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison of simulation results to experimental data.

claim: Cell apoptosis in response to crowding may be a cell-autonomous process rather than specific to cell competition.
source: As the relationship between papo and ρ was fitted using the data from our competition experiments, this also raises the possibility that cell apoptosis in response to crowding is a cell-autonomous process rather than specific to cell competition.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the model results.

claim: Differences in density-mediated apoptosis alone are sufficient to replicate the evolution of cell count and density observed in competition between MDCKWT and MDCKScrib.
source: Overall, differences in density-dependent apoptosis alone are sufficient to replicate the evolution of cell count and density observed in competition between MDCKWT and MDCKScrib as well as the upregulation of MDCKWT division in MDCKScrib-dominated neighbourhoods (Bove et al., 2017), suggesting that mechanical competition represents the dominant mechanism of population change in these experiments.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Mechanical competition represents the dominant mechanism of population change in experiments between MDCKWT and MDCKScrib.
source: Overall, differences in density-dependent apoptosis alone are sufficient to replicate the evolution of cell count and density observed in competition between MDCKWT and MDCKScrib as well as the upregulation of MDCKWT division in MDCKScrib-dominated neighbourhoods (Bove et al., 2017), suggesting that mechanical competition represents the dominant mechanism of population change in these experiments.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results.

claim: The growth rate G controls the time required for elimination and the peak loser cell count but does not affect the outcome of competition.
source: G controlled the time required for elimination and the peak loser cell count but did not affect the outcome of competition with losers being eliminated for all growth rates examined (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B), consistent with simulations of population dynamics based on ordinary differential equations (Basan et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and is consistent with Basan et al., 2009.

claim: Heterotypic adhesion energy Jheterotypic did not appear to change the kinetics or the outcome of mechanical competition.
source: In our simulations, Jheterotypic did not appear to change the kinetics or the outcome of competition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Competition is decreased in the presence of an inhibitor of Rho-kinase (Y27632) that reduces cell contractility in both populations.
source: These results are consistent with experiments showing that competition is decreased in the presence of an inhibitor of Rho-kinase (Y27632) that reduces cell contractility in both populations (Wagstaff et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wagstaff et al., 2016.

claim: In mechanical competition, the normalised count of loser cells reached a maximum around 60 hr before continuously decreasing thereafter.
source: Strikingly, in mechanical competition, the normalised count of loser cells reached a maximum around 60 hr before continuously decreasing thereafter, consistent with our experimental observations in fully mixed (Figure 4B) and partially sorted conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C, Video 9).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model and experimental observations shown in Figure 4B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: By 160 hr, loser cells had been eliminated for all configurations in mechanical competition.
source: By 160 hr, loser cells had been eliminated for all configurations (Figure 6A–C, left-hand column, E).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 6A–C, E.

claim: In biochemical competition, the outcome of competition appeared strongly dependent on initial seeding conditions with large differences in normalised count of losers after 100 hr.
source: In contrast, in biochemical competition, the outcome of competition appeared strongly dependent on initial seeding conditions with large differences in normalised count of losers after 100 hr (Figure 6A–C, right-hand column, D).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 6A–C, D.

claim: Loser cell normalised count was close to 0 for fully mixed seeding in biochemical competition.
source: Indeed, loser cell normalised count was close to 0 for fully mixed seeding but remained larger than 1 for partially and fully sorted seedings.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Loser cell normalised count remained larger than 1 for partially and fully sorted seedings in biochemical competition.
source: Indeed, loser cell normalised count was close to 0 for fully mixed seeding but remained larger than 1 for partially and fully sorted seedings.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: By 200 hr, loser cell count had dropped to 0 in partially sorted seeding in biochemical competition.
source: By 200 hr, loser cell count had dropped to 0 in partially sorted seeding but only decreased gradually for fully sorted seeding (Video 10).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: The kinetics of biochemical competition is sensitive to tissue organisation.
source: This suggests that the kinetics of biochemical competition is sensitive to tissue organisation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results.

claim: When cells reached confluence, entropy of mixing was highest in the fully mixed seeding and lowest in the fully sorted seeding.
source: We found that, when cells reached confluence, entropy of mixing was highest in the fully mixed seeding and lowest in the fully sorted seeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the fully mixed and partially sorted seedings, mixing entropy decreased after overall confluence as the competition progressed.
source: In the fully mixed and partially sorted seedings, mixing entropy decreased after overall confluence as the competition progressed, whereas for fully sorted seeding, mixing entropy stayed constant because the interface between winners and losers maintained its shape over time even though the number of loser cells gradually decreased (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Video 10).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For fully sorted seeding, mixing entropy stayed constant because the interface between winners and losers maintained its shape over time even though the number of loser cells gradually decreased.
source: In the fully mixed and partially sorted seedings, mixing entropy decreased after overall confluence as the competition progressed, whereas for fully sorted seeding, mixing entropy stayed constant because the interface between winners and losers maintained its shape over time even though the number of loser cells gradually decreased (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Video 10).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The time to elimination monotonously increased with cell number in the loser colony.
source: This revealed that the time to elimination monotonously increased with cell number in the colony but that no true steady-state coexistence was reached.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: No true steady-state coexistence was reached in biochemical competition.
source: This revealed that the time to elimination monotonously increased with cell number in the colony but that no true steady-state coexistence was reached.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: The kinetics of biochemical competition is sensitive to changes in parameters that lead to tissue reorganisation, such as the relative magnitude of homotypic and heterotypic adhesion energy.
source: Thus, the kinetics of biochemical competition is sensitive to changes in parameters that lead to tissue reorganisation, such as the relative magnitude of homotypic and heterotypic adhesion energy.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results.

claim: Calibration of model parameters separately for pure populations of winner and loser cells allowed quantitative reproduction of experimentally measured kinetics of cell proliferation, mechanics of tissue homeostasis, the topology of tissue organisation, as well as the cumulative apoptosis and mitosis in each population.
source: Calibration of our model parameters separately for pure populations of winner and loser cells allowed us to quantitatively reproduce the experimentally measured kinetics of cell proliferation, mechanics of tissue homeostasis, the topology of tissue organisation, as well as the cumulative apoptosis and mitosis in each population.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison of simulation results to experimental data.

claim: The increased sensitivity to crowding in loser cells is consistent with the interplay between stress pathways.
source: The latter is directly measured in our experiments (Bove et al., 2017) and is consistent with the increased sensitivity to crowding in loser cells due to interplay between stress pathways (Wagstaff et al., 2016; Kucinski et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bove et al., 2017; Wagstaff et al., 2016; and Kucinski et al., 2017.

claim: Mechanical competition may represent a cell-autonomous phenomenon where each cell type independently seeks to reach its homeostatic density in a dynamically changing environment.
source: A further implication is that mechanical competition may actually represent a cell-autonomous phenomenon where each cell type independently seeks to reach its homeostatic density in a dynamically changing environment.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the model results.

claim: Model parametrisation based on experimental data suggests that loser cells are typically more compressible (or softer) than winners.
source: Our model parametrisation based on experimental data suggests that loser cells are typically more compressible (or softer) than winners.
evidence: The claim is based on the model parametrisation.

claim: In competition assays, loser cells tend to decrease their apical areas more than winners after confluence.
source: As a consequence, in competition assays, loser cells tend to decrease their apical areas more than winners after confluence, as observed in experiments (Wagstaff et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wagstaff et al., 2016.

claim: The decrease in apical area of loser cells in competition implies a concomitant increase in their height.
source: Thus, the decrease in apical area of loser cells in competition implies a concomitant increase in their height, consistent with experimental observations (Wagstaff et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model and is consistent with Wagstaff et al., 2016.

claim: Both contact inhibition of proliferation and planar cell compressibility altered the outcome of mechanical competition by changing the local density attained by the loser cells.
source: Overall, both contact inhibition of proliferation and planar cell compressibility altered the outcome of mechanical competition by changing the local density attained by the loser cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Mechanical competition appears to be primarily regulated by parameters controlling the compressional mechanical energy stored in the system.
source: Thus, mechanical competition appears to be primarily regulated by parameters controlling the compressional mechanical energy stored in the system.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results.

claim: The upregulation of winner cell division in loser neighbourhoods represents an emergent property of the simulation.
source: Therefore, the upregulation of winner cell division in loser neighbourhoods represents an emergent property of our simulation, likely arising from the combination of a higher growth rate and a lower sensitivity to crowding in winner cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: The magnitude of the upregulation of winner cell division in loser neighbourhoods was smaller than in experiments, perhaps pointing to a role for signalling mechanisms accelerating the cell cycle in response to free space.
source: However, the magnitude of this effect was smaller than in experiments, perhaps pointing to a role for signalling mechanisms accelerating the cell cycle in response to free space that was observed in experiments (Gudipaty et al., 2017; Streichan et al., 2014) but not implemented in our simulations.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the comparison of simulation results to experimental data and is supported by citations to Gudipaty et al., 2017 and Streichan et al., 2014.

claim: The interaction between MDCKWT and MDCKScrib cells in experiments can be entirely explained by mechanical competition alone.
source: Overall, our simulations suggest that the interaction between MDCKWT and MDCKScrib cells in our experiments can be entirely explained by mechanical competition alone despite suggestions that signalling mechanisms such as active corralling of losers cells may play a role (Wagstaff et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results and is contrasted with Wagstaff et al., 2016.

claim: Biochemical competition depends on the extent of heterotypic contact between losers and winners.
source: Biochemical competition depends on the extent of heterotypic contact between losers and winners.
evidence: The claim is based on the model implementation.

claim: The kinetics of biochemical competition strongly depends on tissue organisation but is not affected by changes in cell compressibility or contact inhibition.
source: As a result, the kinetics of biochemical competition strongly depends on tissue organisation but is not affected by changes in cell compressibility or contact inhibition (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Two parameters controlled biochemical competition: the heterotypic contact energy and the initial organisation of the tissue.
source: Instead, two parameters controlled biochemical competition: the heterotypic contact energy and the initial organisation of the tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Tissue organisations with greater mixing between the cell types resulted in more rapid elimination of the loser cells.
source: Indeed, tissue organisations with greater mixing between the cell types resulted in more rapid elimination of the loser cells (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model shown in Figure 6.

claim: When the heterotypic contact energy was lower than the homotypic contact energy, this led to more mixing between cell types and more cell competition.
source: Consistent with this, when the heterotypic contact energy was lower than the homotypic contact energy, this led to more mixing between cell types and more cell competition.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Perturbations that promote cohesion of losers protect against elimination, while those that promote intercalation of winners and losers lead to greater loser elimination.
source: Interestingly, experimental evidence has revealed that perturbations that promote cohesion of losers protect against elimination, while those that promote intercalation of winners and losers lead to greater loser elimination (Levayer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levayer et al., 2015.

claim: Clone shape and mixing is set by the ratio of tension within and outside of the clone.
source: In particular, previous work has shown that clone shape and mixing is set by the ratio of tension within and outside of the clone (Bosveld et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bosveld et al., 2016.

claim: The initial organisation of the tissue strongly influenced the kinetics of elimination in biochemical competition.
source: The initial organisation of the tissue strongly influenced the kinetics of elimination, and our simulations revealed a steady increase in the time to elimination with increasing number of cells in the loser colony but no steady coexistence.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Experiments in vivo have revealed a regime of coexistence in biochemical competition.
source: Intriguingly, experiments in vivo have revealed a regime of coexistence (Levayer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levayer et al., 2015.

claim: Mechanical competition is governed by factors that reduce the stored mechanical energy in the system.
source: In summary, our study revealed that mechanical competition is governed by factors that reduce the stored mechanical energy in the system, while biochemical competition is favoured by factors that increase cell intermixing and tissue reorganisation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results.

claim: Biochemical competition is favoured by factors that increase cell intermixing and tissue reorganisation.
source: In summary, our study revealed that mechanical competition is governed by factors that reduce the stored mechanical energy in the system, while biochemical competition is favoured by factors that increase cell intermixing and tissue reorganisation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model results.

claim: Mechanical competition was not affected by tissue organisation.
source: Conversely, mechanical competition was not affected by tissue organisation, whereas biochemical competition was not sensitive to parameters that changed the stored mechanical energy of the tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: Biochemical competition was not sensitive to parameters that changed the stored mechanical energy of the tissue.
source: Conversely, mechanical competition was not affected by tissue organisation, whereas biochemical competition was not sensitive to parameters that changed the stored mechanical energy of the tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the computational model.

claim: MDCKScrib cells spread markedly more than MDCKWT in pure populations.
source: In pure populations, MDCKScrib cells spread markedly more than MDCKWT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D, compare MDCKWT in Video 2 to MDCKScrib in Video 3), consistent with Wagstaff et al., 2016.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D and is consistent with Wagstaff et al., 2016.

claim: In mixed populations dominated by WT cells, MDCKScrib cell area diminished compared to pure populations even prior to confluence.
source: Interestingly, in mixed populations dominated by WT cells, MDCKScrib cell area diminished compared to pure populations even prior to confluence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Transcriptomic data comparing both cell types indicates that MDCKScrib do not express more integrins than MDCKWT.
source: Transcriptomic data comparing both cell types indicates that MDCKScrib do not express more integrins than MDCKWT (Wagstaff et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wagstaff et al., 2016.

claim: MDCKScrib cells grew significantly slower than MDCKWT cells (mean cell cycle times: MDCKScrib ~21.6 hr vs. MDCKWT ~18 hr).
source: The maximum growth rate G was parameterised based on the measured distribution of cell cycle durations prior to confluence (Bove et al., 2017), which showed that losers grew significantly slower than winners (mean cell cycle times: MDCKScrib ~21.6 hr vs. MDCKWT ~18 hr).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from Bove et al., 2017.

claim: In competition experiments, the area of loser cells became significantly smaller than that of winners when monolayers reached high densities post-confluence.
source: Previous experimental work showed that, in competition experiments, the area of loser cells became significantly smaller than that of winners when monolayers reached high densities post-confluence (Wagstaff et al., 2016; Bove et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wagstaff et al., 2016 and Bove et al., 2017.
